APPLICANT

1
REPLY BRIEF
For the reasons explained in the State’s application to vacate, this Court 
should vacate the Sixth Circuit’s stay. Pike’s response fails to establish otherwise.
First, Pike fails to establish that she is likely to prevail on the issue pending 
before the Sixth Circuit—whether her Rule 60(b) motion is a second or successive 
habeas petition. As the State explained in its application, and Judge Griffin 
explained in his dissent, it “clearly” is. Order, No. 26-5864 (6th Cir. Sept. 30, 2026) 
(Griffin, J., dissenting). By Pike’s “own account, the State’s remarks allegedly 
challenge [the Sixth Circuit’s] deference to the court’s postconviction determinations. 
This brings a ‘claim.’” Id. That triggers AEDPA’s limitations on second or successive 
petitions. The district court thus correctly transferred Pike’s Rule 60(b) motion to the 
Sixth Circuit. And because the mitigation-related ineffective-assistance claim Pike 
brings has already been raised, AEDPA bars her from bringing it again. Id.
Pike’s response is to repeat her argument that the State purported to switch 
positions on Pike’s credibility and the veracity of her reported history as a survivor of 
sexual abuse. But again, that all goes to the merits evaluation of her prior habeas 
claim. And again, that is not the proper subject of a Rule 60(b) motion. “When a 
movant asserts . . . that a previous ruling which precluded a merits determination 
was in error[,] he is making a habeas corpus claim.” Gonzalez v. Crosby, 545 U.S. 
524, 532 n.4 (2005). That is what Pike asserts. And that is why she is not likely to 
succeed on the merits of her argument that she brought a proper Rule 60(b) motion.

2
Second, even putting that aside, Pike’s argument rests on a faulty premise. 
Pike is wrong that any credibility finding regarding Pike’s reports of childhood abuse 
impacted the post-conviction decision to deny relief on her mitigation-related 
ineffective-assistance claim. (Indeed, the Tennessee Supreme Court denied Pike’s 
motion to recall the mandate in her post-conviction case based on the same arguments 
she makes here. See Order, Pike v. State, No. E2009-00016-SC-R11-PD (Tenn. Sept. 
29, 2026).) The post-conviction court considered counsel’s decision “not putting 
information in the record related to the petitioner’s traumatic life events such as 
having been raped.” Order, D.9-5, 4475. The court recognized the problematic nature 
of counsel putting on this evidence when Pike’s family members did not believe Pike’s 
reports of these events, which “could have been a very negative factor for the jury as 
it relates to the petitioner’s credibility to other information which she had told other 
witnesses and experts.” Id., 4476. The trial court found counsel’s actions 
reasonable. Id.
Critically, however, the post-conviction court also found no prejudice in view of 
other, cumulative mitigation evidence presented and the overwhelming evidence 
supporting the aggravating circumstances. Id., 4476-77. “Even assuming that all the 
evidence had been presented to the jury that had been presented [on post-conviction 
review], this court cannot find that the jury’s sentencing verdict would have been 
different.” Id., 4477 (emphasis added). And when resolving this issue, the trial court 
did not rely on any credibility finding about Pike’s underlying reports of childhood 
abuse.

3
 Despite Pike’s argument to the contrary, this analysis simply cannot be fairly 
characterized as an “expression of skepticism about the possible impact of the 
evidence” based upon “the State’s arguments.” Response, p. 2. The trial court’s 
“expression of skepticism” was based upon its reasoned assessment of whether 
(1) counsel should have acted differently based upon a review of the full postconviction record, and (2) whether it would have mattered if counsel had. When 
resolving those issues, the trial court took no position on the relative credibility of 
Pike’s reports themselves. The relative credibility of those reports played no role in 
this analysis. Consequently, the federal courts’ habeas orders did not rely on a statecourt order “tainted” by State evidence and argument about Pike’s history of 
childhood abuse. See Pike v. Gross, 936 F.3d 372, 374-75 (6th Cir. 2019) (“Because 
we conclude that the state court’s determination that she is unable to establish 
prejudice on her claims of ineffective assistance of counsel during the penalty phase 
of her capital trial was not an unreasonable application of clearly established federal 
law, we affirm.”); see also id. at 381 (“[B]ecause the jury heard largely the same 
narrative as Pike now presents, the Tennessee Court of Criminal Appeals’ conclusion 
that Pike failed to establish prejudice from Talman’s decision not to call Dr. McCoy 
at the penalty-phase hearing . . .was not an unreasonable application of federal law 
under AEDPA.”).
Third, Pike is wrong to say that the State will suffer no irreparable harm 
because it will only “experience inconvenience.” This callous response gives short 
shrift to the State’s significant interest in finality and totally ignores May Martinez’s

4
three-decade nightmare waiting on justice for her brutally murdered nineteen-yearold daughter. It also ignores the tremendous lengths to which Martinez has gone to 
be present at today’s execution. Although a Florida-based victims advocacy 
organization raised money to cover the cost of Martinez’s trip to Tennessee, it wasn’t 
enough for plane tickets. Steven Hale, Christa Pike’s Imminent Execution Attracts 
Pleas for Mercy, Demands for Justice, and Lurid Interest, Nashville Banner (Sept. 28, 
2026), https://tinyurl.com/zchh33m9. Martinez said she and her husband will be 
making the 600-mile drive to Nashville so they can be at Riverbend for the 
execution. Id. Martinez recently explained that “she needs to witness Pike’s death 
‘so I can remember that she is gone and I don’t have to fear that she’s going to pop up 
somewhere.” Id. Martinez is at the prison this very moment waiting for this Court’s 
decision, waiting on justice for her Colleen.
“Only with an assurance of real finality can the State execute its moral 
judgment in a case” and “the victims of crime move forward knowing the moral 
judgment will be carried out.” Calderon v. Thompson, 523 U.S. 538, 556 
(1998). Contrary to Pike’s response, “[t]o unsettle these expectations is to inflict a 
profound injury.” Id.
Fourth, Pike’s delay is inexcusable. Her Rule 60(b) motion is premised on 
statements of counsel made at a hearing on August 13, 2026. Pike could have filed 
her motion that day, or the next day, or the next day. Instead, she waited 47 days to 
seek relief in the district court—less than 24 hours before her scheduled 
execution. Contrary to Pike’s claims, nothing prevented her from pursuing

5
alternative avenues of relief while she awaited the Tennessee Supreme Court’s 
decision on her pending stay motion in her protocol suit, or the Governor’s decision 
on her clemency petition. This is a textbook example of a “last-minute attempt[] to 
manipulate the judicial process.” Gomez v. U.S. Dist. Ct. for N. Dist. of California, 
503 U.S. 653, 654 (1992). The “abusive delay” must end—now. Id.
CONCLUSION
The Court should grant the application and vacate the stay so that the 
execution may proceed as planned.

6
Respectfully submitted,
Jonathan Skrmetti
Attorney General & Reporter
Madeline W. Clark
Solicitor General
